chunks: From him, from Abdullah ibn Jabalah, from Ali ibn al-Harith, from Bakkar, from Muhammad ibn Shurayh, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who bought the fruit of a palm tree for two or three years, and there was no other palm tree in the land [of the transaction]. He said: 'It is not valid except for one year, and he should not buy it until its validity becomes clear.'

He said: 'And it reached me that he said: Regarding the fruit of trees, there is no harm in buying it if its fruit has become valid.' It was said to him: 'And what is the validity of its fruit?' He said: 'When it sets [forms] after the falling of its blossom.'
ai.seo_question: What is the condition for the validity of selling fruit on trees in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) establishes the principle of 'gharar' (uncertainty) in trade by prohibiting the sale of fruit for multiple years unless its viability is certain, defining validity as the period after the blossom falls and the fruit sets. This ruling, recorded in *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, reflects the Shia juristic emphasis on minimizing risk in agricultural contracts, distinguishing between the uncertain growth phase and the established fruit. The clarification that 'validity' begins post-blossom fall ensures that buyers do not pay for potential but unguaranteed produce.
